The power-log tail integral diverges iff a<2+delta or a=2+delta,b<=1, and its complementary tail gives both clipping constants. A superquadratic globally monotone critical-log-potential example is exact. CHECK.py passed 1131 finite assertions; infinite claims are analytical. For arbitrary eventually well-free U, finite T forces an integrable Boltzmann tail, hence Uprime>=0 eventually; (D Tprime)prime>=-1 and the requisite divergent inverse integral exclude T=x^(gamma+o(1)) with gamma>2+delta. The critical logarithmic example attains the bound. The dual visibility claim uses the exact deficit exp[-Q]: at a=ac+epsilon,b=0 the tail Q is kappa_epsilon*(1+x)^(-epsilon)/epsilon; at a=ac,b=1+eta it is kappa_c*ell(x)^(-eta)/eta. Solving these exact relations gives respectively single-exponential and double-exponential observation radii; after the logarithmic rescalings both give exp[-kappa_c*exp(-s)] with local uniformity in the first case.

originality.rationale: The assessed novel claim is the paired critical finite-distance visibility law for the inverse mean first-passage slope deficit: exact fixed-deficit detection radii, common Gumbel profile, and two sharply different nested distance scales. Keidar-Reuveni-Sokolov 2026 give general homogeneous-D inversion and one cubic example; their theorem combined with the standard Lamperti transformation covers the basic variable-D inversion criterion, which is credited as prerequisite, not claimed new. Menon 2026 and Kim-Netz 2015 cover heterogeneous forward dynamics and different bounded inverse/optimization objects, not the two detection horizons. Published claim searches found no explicit or stronger critical-horizon result. Residual risk: these explicit critical consequences might occur implicitly in older general diffusion/regular-variation literature.

value.rationale: The paired near-critical detection theorem gives exact starting distances at which a failed inverse design becomes observable in relative mean-time slope. A power-exponent error of size epsilon is hidden until single-exponential distance, while a marginal logarithmic-exponent error of size eta is hidden until double-exponential distance; the same Gumbel-type profile governs both. This answers a natural finite-observation identifiability question rather than a routine fixed-parameter substitution. The exact constants and noncommuting limits follow analytically, while robustness under finite-sample noise is unproved.
